```{r setup}
#| code-summary: "Setup: load the simulator, exact solver and formulas"
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
# Quarto's R process may start without a UTF-8 locale; without one, the minus
# signs in tables and chart labels print as "<U+2212>".
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))

for (f in list.files("../R", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)

# The scenario used throughout: American roulette, always betting red,
# $5 base bet, $400 bankroll.
p <- P_AMERICAN
unit <- 5
bankroll <- 400
edge <- 1 - 2 * p  # house edge on an even-money bet, 2/38

# Formatting helpers for numbers quoted in the text
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
usd <- function(x) scales::dollar(round(x), style_negative = "minus")
num <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")

# Chart styling: recessive grid, one highlight color per strategy of interest
col_mart <- "#2a78d6"   # Martingale
col_bold <- "#eb6834"   # bold play
col_other <- "#8a8f98"  # every other strategy (context, labeled directly)
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#e3e5e8"),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#5d6066"),
          plot.title.position = "plot",
          legend.position = "none")
)
strategy_colors <- c("Martingale" = col_mart, "Bold play" = col_bold,
                     "Flat bets" = col_other, "Reverse Martingale" = col_other,
                     "D'Alembert" = col_other, "Fibonacci" = col_other)

set.seed(2024)
```

```{r compute}
#| code-summary: "Run every calculation the report quotes"
# 1. Exact answers for each strategy trying to turn $400 into $800
exact <- compare_exact(all_strategies(), bankroll, p, unit, goal = 2 * bankroll)

# 2. The same question by simulation, 10,000 players per strategy
n_sim <- 10000
sims <- lapply(all_strategies(), function(s) {
  simulate_many(n_sim, s, bankroll, p, unit, goal = 2 * bankroll)
})
sim_summary <- data.frame(
  strategy = sapply(all_strategies(), `[[`, "name"),
  sim_p_goal = sapply(sims, function(d) mean(d$reached_goal)),
  sim_result = sapply(sims, function(d) mean(d$result))
)
both <- merge(exact, sim_summary, by = "strategy")

# 3. The original experiment: Martingale players who never walk away
broke <- simulate_many(n_sim, martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, goal = Inf)
share_ahead <- mean(broke$peak > bankroll)

m <- exact[exact$strategy == "Martingale", ]
b <- exact[exact$strategy == "Bold play", ]
f <- exact[exact$strategy == "Flat bets", ]
```

::: findings
**What this project finds** (American roulette, betting red, $400 bankroll, trying to reach $800)

1. **Every system loses the same share of what it bets.** Your average loss is
   the house edge (`r pct(edge, 2)`) times the total amount you bet. This holds exactly
   for all six strategies tested. The Martingale doesn't beat the edge. It makes
   you bet `r round(m$exp_wagered / bankroll, 1)` times your bankroll.
2. **A single bold bet beats the Martingale.** One $400 bet on red doubles your money
   `r pct(b$p_goal)` of the time and costs `r usd(b$exp_result)` on average. The
   Martingale manages `r pct(m$p_goal)` and costs `r usd(m$exp_result)`.
3. **A high win rate is the wrong thing to measure.** Aim for a small profit and the
   Martingale wins most sessions, yet it still loses money on average. That pattern
   (frequent small gains, rare ruinous losses) shows up well beyond the casino.
:::

## The promise

In the carnival of 1754, Giacomo Casanova was gambling in Venice with money
belonging to his lover. His memoirs record that, "playing the martingale, and
doubling my stakes continuously, I won every day during the remainder of the
carnival." Not long after, the story ends the way it usually does: "I still
played on the martingale, but with such bad luck that I was soon left without a
sequin." [@casanova]

The system is simple. Bet one unit on red. If you lose, double the bet. When you
finally win, that one win recovers every loss in the streak plus one unit of profit,
and you start again. Since red has to come up eventually, it *feels* like a machine
for printing small, steady wins.

```{r single-run}
#| fig-cap: "One simulated Martingale player who never walks away."
set.seed(11)
run <- simulate_player(martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, path = TRUE)
run_df <- data.frame(spin = seq_along(run$cash), cash = run$cash)

ggplot(run_df, aes(spin, cash)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bankroll, color = "#5d6066", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(color = col_mart, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 60, y = bankroll, label = "Starting bankroll",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6, color = "#5d6066", size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Spin", y = "Cash in hand",
       title = "The bankroll creeps up, then a losing streak wipes it out",
       subtitle = "$5 base bet, $400 bankroll, betting red on American roulette")
```

That is what most players see. Among `r num(n_sim)` simulated players who use the
Martingale and never walk away, **`r pct(share_ahead)` were ahead of their starting
$400 at some point**. The median player's best moment was `r usd(median(broke$peak))`.
In the end every one of them lost the whole bankroll, but that isn't a finding: a
player who never stops in a game with a house edge will always go broke eventually.
The useful question is what happens to players who *do* plan to stop.

## Why no system can win

Here is the rule that settles it. On every spin, a bet on red loses `r pct(edge, 2)`
of its stake on average. A betting system decides *how much* to stake and *when to
stop*, but it can't change the edge on any single spin. So over a whole session:

$$
\text{average result} = -\text{house edge} \times \text{average total amount bet}
$$

This is Wald's identity applied to gambling, and Ethier [-@ethier, p. 298] proves it
holds for every betting system. As Epstein puts it, all betting systems
"lead ultimately to the same mathematical expectation of gain per unit amount
wagered" [@epstein, p. 52].

The project doesn't take this on trust. Its exact solver calculates each strategy's
average result from the distribution of final bankrolls, without using the house
edge, and the identity comes out to within rounding error for every strategy
(it is also one of the automated tests):

```{r identity}
#| fig-cap: "Exact results for six strategies, each trying to turn $400 into $800."
#| fig-height: 4.8
# Labels are placed by hand, clear of the dashed line: offsets in dollars
# from each point, and which side of the label anchors to that position.
label_pos <- data.frame(
  strategy = c("Bold play", "Martingale", "Reverse Martingale", "Fibonacci", "D'Alembert", "Flat bets"),
  dx = c(150, 150, -150, 150, -150, -200),
  dy = c(8, 25, -25, 25, -25, 0),
  hjust = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1)
)
exact_plot <- merge(exact, label_pos, by = "strategy")

ggplot(exact_plot, aes(exp_wagered, exp_result)) +
  geom_abline(slope = -edge, intercept = 0, color = "#5d6066", linewidth = 0.4,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(color = strategy), size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(aes(x = exp_wagered + dx, y = exp_result + dy, label = strategy, hjust = hjust),
            size = 3.6, color = "#1c1d1f") +
  annotate("text", x = 3900, y = -60, label = "Dashed line: average result = −5.26% × amount bet",
           hjust = 0, color = "#5d6066", size = 3.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) scales::dollar(x, style_negative = "minus")) +
  labs(x = "Average total amount bet in the session",
       y = "Average result",
       title = "Every strategy sits on the same line",
       subtitle = "The more you bet in total, the more you lose. Nothing else matters to the average.")
```

```{r identity-table}
exact |>
  arrange(desc(p_goal)) |>
  transmute(Strategy = strategy,
            `Average total bet` = usd(exp_wagered),
            `Average result` = usd(exp_result),
            `Result ÷ amount bet` = pct(exp_result / exp_wagered, 2),
            `Average spins` = num(exp_spins)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The word *martingale* has a second life here. In 1939 the French mathematician
Jean Ville borrowed the gamblers' term for a new idea in probability theory: a fair
game in which, whatever you know so far, your expected future fortune equals your
present one [@mansuy]. Joseph Doob developed the idea into one of the central tools of
modern probability. A central result, the *optional stopping theorem*, says that
with finite money and finite time, no rule for sizing bets or choosing when to stop can turn a
fair game into a favourable one, let alone an unfavourable game like roulette. The
system gave the mathematics its name, and the mathematics shows why the system can't work.

## Why it feels like it works anyway

The Martingale isn't fooling people with nothing. It really does win small amounts most
of the time. It fails only when a losing streak runs longer than the bankroll can cover,
and that streak is rare on any given spin.

With a $5 base bet, a $400 bankroll covers
`r max_covered_streak(bankroll, unit)` losses in a row
($5 + $10 + … + $160 = $315). The seventh bet would be $320 with only $85 left.
Seven reds missed in a row has probability
`r pct((1 - p)^7, 2)`, so it almost never happens on a given spin. Over a long
evening it becomes likely:

```{r streak}
#| fig-cap: "Exact probability, from the run-length formula in R/formulas.R."
spins <- 1:1000
streak_df <- data.frame(spins = spins,
                        prob = sapply(spins, function(n) prob_losing_streak(7, n, 1 - p)))
p500 <- streak_df$prob[500]

ggplot(streak_df, aes(spins, prob)) +
  geom_line(color = col_mart, linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("point", x = 500, y = p500, color = col_mart, size = 2.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 500, y = p500, label = paste0(pct(p500, 0), " by spin 500"),
           hjust = -0.15, vjust = 1.4, size = 3.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Spins played", y = "Chance of at least one 7-loss streak",
       title = "Rare on any spin, likely over an evening",
       subtitle = "Probability of seeing 7 or more losses in a row on red, American roulette")
```

Can a bigger bankroll fix this? Each extra loss you want to cover **doubles** the money
you need, but only cuts the chance of the fatal streak by a factor of
`r round(1 - p, 3)`. Meanwhile the average loss stays the same share of everything you
bet. Casinos also set table maximums, which stop the doubling at a fixed point no matter
how rich the player is [@pflaumer]. The simulator models this: when the next doubled bet
would exceed the limit, the player takes the loss and starts again at the base bet.

```{r bankroll-table}
streaks <- 4:12
tibble(`Losses covered` = streaks,
       `Bankroll needed` = usd(unit * (2^streaks - 1)),
       `Chance the fatal streak appears within 500 spins` =
         pct(sapply(streaks + 1, function(k) prob_losing_streak(k, 500, 1 - p)))) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "rrr")
```

## If you must gamble

Suppose the goal is modest and concrete: turn $400 into $800, then go home. Which
strategy gives the best chance?

```{r compare}
#| fig-cap: "Exact probabilities. Points show 10,000 simulated players per strategy."
#| fig-height: 4
cmp <- both |> arrange(p_goal) |> mutate(strategy = factor(strategy, levels = strategy))

ggplot(cmp, aes(p_goal, strategy)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = p_goal, yend = strategy, color = strategy),
               linewidth = 2.2, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = sim_p_goal), shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "#1c1d1f", size = 2.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(p_goal < 0.01, pct(p_goal, 2), pct(p_goal))),
            hjust = -0.25, size = 3.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.56), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Chance of doubling $400 before going broke", y = NULL,
       title = "One big bet beats every progression",
       subtitle = "Bars: exact solver. White dots: simulation. They agree to within sampling error.") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r compare-table}
both |>
  arrange(desc(p_goal)) |>
  transmute(Strategy = strategy,
            `Chance of doubling (exact)` = pct(p_goal, 2),
            `Simulated (10,000 players)` = pct(sim_p_goal, 2),
            `Average result (exact)` = usd(exp_result),
            `Simulated average` = usd(sim_result)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The winner is **bold play**: bet whatever gets you to the goal in one win, or everything
you have if that's less. Here that means a single $400 bet on red. It succeeds with
probability exactly 18/38 = `r pct(b$p_goal)` and costs `r usd(b$exp_result)` on average,
because you only expose $400 to the house edge once.

This isn't a quirk of the scenario. Dubins and Savage proved in *How to Gamble If You
Must* that in a game where the odds are against you, bold play maximises the chance of
reaching a fixed goal [@dubins-savage]. The identity above shows why. When a session
can only end broke or exactly at the goal (true for flat bets, the Martingale and bold
play), the average final bankroll is simply the goal times the chance of reaching it.
Combining that with the identity gives:

$$
P(\text{reach goal}) = \frac{\text{bankroll} - \text{house edge} \times \text{average total amount bet}}{\text{goal}}
$$

For the Martingale: ($400 − 5.26% × `r usd(m$exp_wagered)`) ÷ $800 =
`r pct(m$p_goal)`. Every extra dollar a strategy bets on the way to the goal costs it
a fixed slice of its chance of getting there, so the strategy that bets least wins most
often. Flat $5 bets are the opposite
extreme. They need about `r num(f$exp_spins)` spins on average, and the edge grinds the
chance of doubling down to `r pct(f$p_goal, 2)`.

From this angle the Martingale is a timid version of bold play. Each round risks a
growing amount in the hope of winning one unit back, so it bets much more in total
than one bold bet would, without improving the odds. The reverse Martingale reaches the
goal less often, but it loses less on average than the Martingale because it bets
less overall.

None of this makes roulette a good investment. Every strategy in the table has a negative
average. Bold play is simply the least bad way to chase a fixed target.

## A high win rate is the wrong metric

The Martingale's real appeal is its win rate. Aim for a small enough profit and it
"works" most of the time:

```{r win-rate}
#| fig-cap: "Exact results for a $400 bankroll aiming for a profit of $25 to $400."
#| fig-height: 4.4
targets <- seq(25, 400, by = 25)
wr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(targets, function(t) {
  rbind(
    cbind(target = t, strategy = "Martingale",
          as.data.frame(solve_exact(martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, bankroll + t)[c("p_goal", "exp_result")])),
    cbind(target = t, strategy = "Bold play",
          as.data.frame(solve_exact(bold_play(), bankroll, p, unit, bankroll + t)[c("p_goal", "exp_result")]))
  )
}))
m25 <- wr[wr$target == 25 & wr$strategy == "Martingale", ]

# Label each line at its right end: bold play above its line, Martingale below.
end_labels <- wr |> filter(target == max(targets)) |>
  mutate(vjust = ifelse(strategy == "Bold play", -0.8, 1.8))
g1 <- ggplot(wr, aes(target, p_goal, color = strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = end_labels, aes(label = strategy, vjust = vjust), hjust = 1, size = 3.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Profit target", y = NULL, title = "Chance of hitting the target")
g2 <- ggplot(wr, aes(target, exp_result, color = strategy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#5d6066", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = end_labels, aes(label = strategy, vjust = vjust), hjust = 1, size = 3.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) scales::dollar(x, style_negative = "minus")) +
  labs(x = "Profit target", y = NULL, title = "Average result")
g1 + g2 + plot_annotation(
  title = "Win often, still lose on average",
  subtitle = "Martingale vs bold play, $400 bankroll, American roulette",
  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
                plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#5d6066"))
)
```

A Martingale player aiming to win $25 succeeds **`r pct(m25$p_goal)`** of the time.
The other `r pct(1 - m25$p_goal)` of sessions lose close to the whole $400, so the
average result is still `r usd(m25$exp_result)`. Someone who judged the strategy by
its win rate, or by a short run of sessions, would think it was excellent.

That payoff shape (usually win a little, occasionally lose almost everything) is not
unique to roulette. The examples below are **analogies, not claims that markets are
roulette wheels**. What they share is the shape of the payoff, not the odds.

- **Doubling down at Barings.** Brown and Steenbeek studied exchange data from Nick
  Leeson's trading in Singapore and found that he "continuously doubled his position
  as prices were falling". The losses, around US$1.4 billion, brought down Barings
  Bank in 1995 [@brown-steenbeek]. Their warning applies to any doubler: the eventual
  loss "is preceded by a period of high returns with low volatility", which looks
  like skill until it isn't.
- **Betting on calm markets.** Short-volatility exchange-traded products profit
  steadily while stock markets stay calm. On 5 February 2018 a jump in volatility
  caused a one-day loss of more than 90% in their value [@augustin-volmageddon].
- **"Martingale" trading bots.** Automated strategies that add to a losing position at
  set intervals are commissioned for retail forex platforms such as MetaTrader under
  that name [@mql5-grid]. They follow the same logic as the roulette system, and they
  carry the same risk.

The lesson for anyone evaluating a strategy, model or product metric: **a success rate
says nothing about the size of the failures.** Look at the expected value and the tail of
the distribution, and be wary of any evaluation window that may simply not have been long
enough to catch the rare bad outcome. The first version of this project made a related
mistake. It reported that every simulated player went broke as if that were a finding,
when the setup guaranteed it.

## How the numbers were produced

Every result comes from two independent engines that share the same strategy
definitions (`R/strategies.R`):

- **Simulation** (`R/simulate.R`): plays each session spin by spin with random outcomes.
- **Exact solver** (`R/exact.R`): with a fixed goal, a session is a Markov chain whose state
  is (cash in hand, the strategy's memory, such as the current bet). The solver lists
  every reachable state and solves the chain's linear equations for the probability of
  reaching the goal, the expected amount bet, the expected number of spins and the
  expected final bankroll. No random numbers are involved.

The test suite (`tests/testthat/`) checks the two engines against each other and against
published results:

| Check | Compared against |
|---|---|
| Flat betting | The classical gambler's-ruin formula |
| Bold play | The Dubins–Savage recursion |
| Every strategy, two wheels, with and without table limits | Average result = −edge × amount bet |
| Every strategy in a fair game | Average result of exactly zero |
| Martingale round statistics with a table limit | Pflaumer (2019), Table 1 |
| Losing-streak probabilities | Brute-force enumeration of all 1,024 ten-spin sequences |
| Simulation vs exact solver, all six strategies | Agreement within four standard errors |

## Assumptions and limits

- The wheel is fair and spins are independent. Every bet is on an even-money chance
  (red/black), with no *la partage* or *en prison* rules. Those rules halve the house
  edge on European wheels and would shrink every loss in this report, but they don't
  change the conclusions.
- Bets come in whole $5 units and must be at least the base bet, except that a player
  who can't cover the next bet stakes everything they have left.
- The headline scenario ($400 bankroll, $800 goal) is one choice among many. The ordering
  of strategies is not specific to it: bold play's advantage is a theorem. The exact
  percentages are specific to it, and the explorer lets you change them.
- The finance examples illustrate a payoff shape. They are not a model of any market.
